title: Backtracking
tagline: Try, recurse, undo. The brute-force-with-pruning template that solves permutations, combinations, n-queens, and sudoku.
intro:
Backtracking is systematic brute force: explore every candidate by building a partial solution one choice at a time, and **undo** the last choice when it leads nowhere. It's depth-first search over the tree of all possible decisions, with the key addition of **pruning** — abandoning a branch the moment it can't lead to a valid answer.

The whole pattern collapses into three steps repeated recursively: **choose** (make a move), **explore** (recurse), **un-choose** (undo the move so you can try the next one). Get that rhythm in your fingers and every 'generate all ...' problem — subsets, permutations, combinations, partitions — plus constraint puzzles like n-queens and sudoku become the same template with a different 'is this choice valid?' check.

This module gives you the universal template, the choose/explore/unchoose mechanics, how to handle duplicates, and how pruning turns an impossible search into a feasible one.
objectives: Recognise 'generate all / find all valid configurations' as backtracking
Write the universal choose / explore / un-choose template
Generate subsets, permutations, and combinations correctly
Handle duplicate elements without producing duplicate results
Prune invalid branches early to cut the search space
Estimate backtracking complexity (it's exponential — know the bound)

signals: "Generate / find ALL ..." subsets, permutations, combinations, partitions
Constraint-satisfaction puzzles: n-queens, sudoku, word search
"How many ways" where you must enumerate (not just count via DP)
Decisions form a tree and invalid partials can be abandoned early
antiSignals: Only the COUNT or the OPTIMAL value is needed, with overlapping subproblems → DP
A greedy choice provably works → greedy is far faster
n is large and you'd enumerate exponentially with no pruning → reconsider

sections.heading: The big idea in plain words
sections.body:
Backtracking is exploring a maze while dropping breadcrumbs. You walk forward making choices; when you hit a dead end, you walk back to the last fork, pick up your breadcrumb (undo that choice), and try a different door. Try, explore, undo - over and over, until you've covered every path.

Example: all subsets of `{1, 2}`. Choose 1, and you have {1}; go deeper and add 2 for {1, 2}; then back out. Now skip 1 and choose 2 for {2}. Collecting along the way gives {}, {1}, {1, 2}, {2}. That little 'undo' step is the whole magic - it lets you reuse the same path to try the next option instead of starting over.

sections.heading: The three moves
sections.body:
Every backtracking solution is built from three actions wrapped in recursion.

| Step | Action | Code shape |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Choose** | Add a candidate to the current path | `path.add(x)` |
| **Explore** | Recurse with that choice in place | `backtrack(...)` |
| **Un-choose** | Remove it so the next candidate is clean | `path.remove(x)` |

The un-choose step is what makes it 'backtracking' — you rewind state so the same `path` object can be reused across all branches. Forget it and your results bleed into each other.

callouts.text: The #1 backtracking bug: forgetting to undo the choice (or recording a reference to a mutable `path` instead of a copy). Add a snapshot to results: `res.add(new ArrayList<>(path))`, then undo.

sections.heading: The decision tree mental model
sections.body:
Picture the search as a tree: the root is the empty partial solution, each edge is a choice, each leaf is a complete candidate. Backtracking is a DFS over this tree.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["[] empty"] --> B["choose 1"]
  A --> C["choose 2"]
  A --> D["choose 3"]
  B --> B1["1,2"]
  B --> B2["1,3"]
  C --> C1["2,3"]
```

**Pruning** is cutting off a subtree the instant the partial solution is doomed — e.g. in n-queens, the moment two queens attack each other, you don't explore that branch's millions of leaves. Good pruning is the difference between 'runs instantly' and 'never finishes'.

sections.heading: The universal template
sections.body: Memorise this skeleton; every problem just fills in 'is this a complete solution?', 'what are the candidate choices?', and 'is this choice valid?'.

sections.heading: Subsets vs permutations vs combinations
sections.body:
These three differ only in how the loop advances and whether order matters.

| Problem | Order matters? | Reuse elements? | Key loop detail |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Subsets** | no | no | recurse with `i+1`, record every node |
| **Combinations** (k of n) | no | no | recurse with `i+1`, record at depth k |
| **Permutations** | yes | no | loop from 0, track a `used[]` set |
| **Combination sum** (reuse) | no | yes | recurse with `i` (not i+1) to reuse |

The `start` index vs `used[]` array distinction is the crux: a `start` index prevents revisiting earlier elements (so order doesn't matter); a `used[]` set lets you pick any unused element (so order does).

sections.heading: Handling duplicates
sections.body: When the input has duplicate values, you'll generate duplicate results unless you guard against it. The fix: **sort the input first**, then in the loop, skip a candidate if it equals the previous one *and the previous one wasn't used at this level*. This keeps one canonical ordering of equal elements and eliminates repeats without a hash set.

interviewTalking: Frame it as constrained brute force: "I need to enumerate all valid configurations, so I'll backtrack — choose a candidate, recurse, then undo so I can try the next. I'll prune branches that already violate the constraints." Be explicit about the snapshot/undo pair, because that's where bugs live. Acknowledge the complexity honestly: "This is exponential — O(2^n) for subsets, O(n!) for permutations — which is expected since the output itself is that large; pruning keeps it tractable for the given constraints."
commonMistakes: Forgetting to un-choose (undo) the last move, corrupting sibling branches
Storing a reference to the mutable `path` instead of a copy/snapshot in results
Using a `start` index when order matters (permutations need a `used[]` set)
Not sorting before the duplicate-skip check, so duplicates slip through
Recursing with `i` instead of `i+1` when elements can't be reused (or vice versa)
Missing pruning, so the search explores doomed branches and times out
complexityNotes: Backtracking is exponential by nature: subsets O(2^n), permutations O(n!·n), combinations O(C(n,k)·k). Space is O(n) for the recursion depth and current path (excluding the output). Pruning reduces the constant/branching factor but not the worst-case class.
